newsitem.title: INDIA: India's new premier faces confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: India's new premier faces confidence vote.

text.p: India's new prime minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, prepared to face a vote of confidence on Tuesday at the head of a centre-left coalition that changed its leader to win back a former ally.
The United Front announced a new coordination committee with the Congress party, which triggered a political crisis on March 30 by withdrawing vital support to then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda.

The 15-party alliance under Gujral, a 77-year-old Marxist turned social democrat, was expected to prove easily that it commands a parliamentary majority after patching things up with the Congress party.
Parliament was scheduled to convene at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) to debate India's third government in 11 months, formed to avoid mid-term elections. Voting was expected at the end of the day.
Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition was cobbled together with Congress support in June last year to oust a 12-day-old government formed by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The BJP controls 193 votes in the 545-member lower house of parliament. The Congress has 140 and the United Front 178.
When the Congress withdrew support to Deve Gowda, it accused him of not containing the BJP.
Deve Gowda lost power in a confidence vote on April 11. The alliance then elected Gujral as its new leader under a truce with the Congress aimed at avoiding elections.
The transition was smooth. "I have no regrets, nor a sense of frustration or rancour," Deve Gowda said in a farewell speech.
Within hours of assuming office, Gujral showed that he would retain the political soul of his predecessor.
Gujral told industry leaders that he would sustain Deve Gowda's economic reforms and retain his government's tax-cutting budget for 1997/98 (April-March), which awaits parliamentary approval.
The ministry Gujral named was largely the same as the previous one.
But P.Chidambaram, the finance minister who presented the February 28 budget, was missing because his regional Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party pulled out of the alliance amid political friction.
Chidambaram's TMC decided not to join the new government after party leader G.K. Moopanar lost out in the prime ministerial race in a close finish.

Gujral kept the finance minister's job vacant, and United Front officials expressed the hope that Chidambaram and his party colleagues would change their minds. TMC lawmakers said the party would "go to the people" to decide.

The goatee-bearded Gujral, who was foreign minister in the ousted cabinet, reaffirmed his desire for friendly relations with all nations, particularly South Asian neighbours, who welcomed him with enthusiasm that went beyond the usual formalities.

Himself born in Lahore, now in Pakistan, before the division of British-ruled India, Gujral has scored key diplomatic gains in the past 10 months, reviving stalled high-level talks with arch-rival Pakistan and sealing a water treaty with Dhaka.
